# On Thread

The word *clue* used to be *clew*, and a clew was a ball of yarn. That's the whole story: when Theseus went into the labyrinth to kill the Minotaur, Ariadne gave him a ball of thread to unwind behind him so he could find his way out again. The thread was the clew. Over centuries the object dissolved into the abstraction, the way a photograph left in the sun goes pale and then goes white, and now when a detective says she has a clue she is unknowingly holding one end of a string that runs back to a girl standing at the mouth of a maze in Crete.

I find this delightful in a way I have some difficulty defending. It isn't useful. Knowing the etymology of *clue* does not help you find your keys. And there's a well-known trap here — the etymological fallacy, the belief that a word's origin is its "real" meaning, that everything since is drift and corruption. That's plainly false. Words mean what they're used to mean. *Nice* came from Latin *nescius*, ignorant, and traveled through foolish, wanton, shy, fastidious, precise, and finally arrived at pleasant, and nobody is served by insisting that when you call a dinner party nice you are calling it stupid. Language is not a museum. It's a river that people keep drinking from.

And yet. There's something in the fossil record that I keep going back to. *Muscle* is Latin *musculus*, little mouse, because somebody watched a bicep move under skin and thought: mouse. *Sarcophagus* is Greek for flesh-eater, because a certain limestone from Assos was believed to consume the bodies laid in it. *Companion* is someone you eat bread with. *Disaster* is a bad star. Every one of these is a moment where a person, long dead, looked at something without a name and reached for the nearest thing they knew, and the reach stuck. The metaphor hardened into a fact. We walk around all day on a floor made of other people's poetry, and we can't feel it, because the floor is what feeling stands on.

Occasionally the floor gives a little. I like the word *threshold*, whose origin nobody is quite sure of — perhaps something to do with threshing, with the board that kept the grain from spilling out the door — and I like that the uncertainty sits right there at the entrance, the one place where you'd want to know exactly where you are.

---

The false etymologies are almost better than the true ones. There's the famous story that *sincere* comes from *sine cera*, "without wax," referring to honest sculptors who didn't patch flaws in marble with wax filler. It's a beautiful story and it is not true; the word almost certainly comes from *sincerus*, meaning clean or pure, whose deeper roots are murky. But the wax story survives because it *works* — it's shaped like a truth. It explains a moral quality by means of a craft, it has a villain (the fraudulent sculptor) and a virtue (the honest stone), and it makes an abstraction touchable.

I notice I'm not entirely sorry the wax story is false. A true etymology tells you where a word came from. A false one that persists tells you what people *want* the word to mean, which is a different and possibly more interesting kind of data. It's the difference between a fossil and a dream about a fossil. Both are evidence, just of different things.

There's a version of intellectual hygiene that would have us stamp out every one of these and I understand the impulse — a lot of nonsense propagates through exactly this channel, the story too good to check. But I think you can hold a beautiful wrong thing in one hand and the correction in the other, and be richer than if you held only one. The trick is not to confuse the hands.

---

What I actually want to talk about is thread, and I got here by way of the clew, which is a fitting way to arrive.

Most of what has ever existed is gone. This is such an obvious statement that it's hard to feel. But consider Sappho, who was, by the reckoning of the ancient world, one of the great poets — the Tenth Muse, they called her, and the Alexandrians collected her work into nine books. What we have now is one complete poem, one nearly complete, and then fragments: a few hundred scraps, many of them a single word, preserved either because some grammarian quoted them to illustrate a dialect feature, or because a strip of papyrus was used to stuff a mummified crocodile in Egypt and got dug up two thousand years later at Oxyrhynchus.

Anne Carson's translation, *If Not, Winter*, renders the gaps as brackets. Page after page of white space with a word floating in it. "]" then "you burn me" then "]". The effect is not, as you'd expect, one of frustration. It's the opposite. The brackets do something to the surviving words — they charge them. "You burn me" alone on a page, with the roar of the missing poem all around it, hits harder than it plausibly did in its original context, where it was probably the third line of something with a beginning and an end and a normal shape.

This makes me uneasy, actually. I am admiring an artifact of catastrophe. The beauty I'm responding to was manufactured by fire, mold, insects, indifference, and the specific decision of some Byzantine scribe that this scroll wasn't worth recopying. It feels like praising a bombed cathedral for its improved sightlines. Sappho did not write in fragments. She wrote poems, and someone lost them, and now I'm calling the loss aesthetic.

But I don't think I can talk myself out of it either. The response is real. And maybe what's actually happening is that the fragments make visible a condition that's always true and usually hidden: that we never get the whole of anything. Every text arrives partial. Every person you know, you know in fragments — a few hundred hours out of a life, a handful of moods, the parts they showed you. The brackets are just honest about it.

---

Here is my favorite object in the world, or one of them: the Archimedes Palimpsest.

In the tenth century, somebody in Constantinople copied out several treatises by Archimedes, including one called *The Method of Mechanical Theorems* that survives nowhere else. Two hundred years later, parchment being expensive and Archimedes being, one assumes, less immediately useful than liturgy, a monk scraped the pages, cut them in half, turned them ninety degrees, and wrote a prayer book over the top. He erased one of the foundational documents of human mathematics to make a devotional text he probably used every day.

And then the whole thing sat around for eight hundred years, was damaged by fire and mold and forged Byzantine portraits painted on by a twentieth-century owner trying to raise its price, and then, starting in 1998, was read anyway — with ultraviolet, with X-ray fluorescence at a synchrotron, the iron in the old ink lighting up under the new. Archimedes came back up through the prayers.

I love this because it refuses to resolve into a simple story. The monk is not a villain; he needed a prayer book, parchment was scarce, and by scraping and rebinding he accidentally ensured the survival of pages that would otherwise have rotted with the rest. The destruction was the preservation. The text was saved by being erased.

And there's the word itself: *palimpsest*, from Greek, "scraped again." Another dead metaphor, but this one has been so useful that it's climbed back out of the grave — we use it now for cities, for memory, for anything where the old layer shows through. The word became a tool for seeing a pattern that exists everywhere once you have a name for it. Which is, I suppose, what words are for.

---

All of this is really about maintenance, which is the thing I actually keep circling.

There was an essay — Andrew Russell and Lee Vinsel, in *Aeon*, around 2016 — called "Hail the Maintainers," arguing that we have wildly overweighted innovation relative to the far larger and more consequential work of keeping existing things running. Most of the labor in any technological society is maintenance. Most of the labor in a household is maintenance. Most of what makes a friendship last twenty years is maintenance. And it's almost invisible, because success looks like nothing happening. The bridge doesn't fall down. The water is drinkable. Your friend, who is going through something, receives a text from you on the right Tuesday.

The reason it's invisible is structural, not accidental. Innovation produces an event — a launch, a discovery, a before and after. Maintenance produces a non-event. You cannot photograph the absence of a collapse. There's no ribbon-cutting for the bridge that continued to stand. So the entire class of activity that keeps the world habitable is systematically underdescribed, and therefore underpaid, and therefore, often, under-performed, until the bridge does fall down, at which point everyone has a great deal to say.

I think about this in relation to the fragments. We think of loss as something that happens — a fire, a flood, a sack of a city. Dramatic. But almost all loss is a maintenance failure. Sappho didn't burn in a single afternoon. She was copied less, and then less, and then not at all, over centuries, by people who each individually made a defensible allocation of scarce parchment and scribal hours. The extinction of a text is usually not an event. It's the accumulated weight of a very large number of Tuesdays on which no one recopied it.

That's a bleaker thought than I intended when I started this paragraph. Let me set against it: the same logic runs the other way. Everything that *has* survived did so because a very large number of people, most of them unrecorded, did the boring thing on the boring day. Somebody dusted. Somebody recopied. Somebody, in a monastery, in a bad century, kept the roof on.

---

The Ise Grand Shrine in Japan is rebuilt every twenty years. Not repaired — rebuilt, entirely, on an adjacent plot, using the same techniques, by carpenters trained by the carpenters who did it last time. Then the old one is dismantled and its timbers distributed to other shrines. This has been going on, with some interruptions, for something over a millennium. The current building is new. The shrine is thirteen hundred years old.

Which is it? This is the Ship of Theseus problem, except that the Japanese answer arrived before the Greek puzzle was fashionable in the West and it isn't presented as a puzzle at all. It's a practice. The thing being preserved is not the wood. It's the knowing-how — the joinery, the sourcing of the cypress, the sequence of rituals — which can only be preserved by being *used*, because a technique that isn't practiced for a hundred years is not a technique, it's a document, and documents lie about how to do things in ways you only discover when you try.

Twenty years is roughly the interval at which a young carpenter becomes an old one. The rebuilding cycle is calibrated to human apprenticeship. It's a memory system built out of bodies.

I find that I keep being drawn to this class of thing: preservation-by-doing rather than preservation-by-storing. A recipe is not a cuisine. A score is not a performance. A dictionary is not a language. You can put a language in a book and the book will sit on a shelf being, in some technical sense, complete, and the language will still be dead, because a language is a thing that happens between people and not a thing that sits.

---

Back to thread, because I promised.

There's a Japanese textile tradition called *boro* — from a word meaning rags, tatters. Cotton was scarce in the north; families patched garments with indigo scraps, then patched the patches, layer on layer, sometimes for generations, stitching everything down with rows of running stitch called *sashiko*. The results are now in museums. Objects made entirely out of poverty and necessary repair, and they are, by any standard I can bring to bear, gorgeous — deep blue fields crossed by white stitching, every patch a different age, the whole thing a record in cloth of every winter it survived.

And the *kintsugi* pots, of course, which everyone knows about now: broken ceramics rejoined with lacquer dusted with gold, so the break is emphasized rather than hidden. The metaphor has been so thoroughly extracted from these objects — resilience, scars as beauty, all of it slightly worn smooth by repetition on inspirational posters — that it's easy to forget the pots are also just *pots*, made by someone who wanted to keep using a bowl.

That's the thing I keep wanting to hold onto. The bowl was mended because someone wanted to eat out of it. The coat was patched because it was cold. The shrine is rebuilt because it's a shrine. The meaning came afterward and from outside; the act itself was practical, local, and undertaken by someone with something else on their mind.

I suspect that's true of most of what we later find beautiful. Nobody makes a fossil on purpose.

---

I've been writing about thread for a while now and I should probably say why. It's a good image for a couple of things I can't otherwise get at.

One: continuity that doesn't depend on any single piece persisting. A thread is long and thin and can be spliced. The rope that holds the boat is not one fiber; no fiber runs the whole length; the strength is entirely in the overlap. Which is how traditions work, and languages, and families, and how anything at all gets across a gap longer than one lifetime.

Two: thread is what you use when the alternative is that things fall apart. It's the technology of holding-together, the least glamorous and most necessary invention, older than the wheel by tens of thousands of years. Someone twisted plant fiber and suddenly there were nets, bags, bows, clothes, boats, the whole apparatus. And it rots. Almost none of it survives archaeologically. The most important material in human prehistory is functionally invisible in the record, and we infer it from the needles and the impressions in clay and the fact that people got to Australia.

Three: it's the clew. It's what you unwind behind you so that when you're deep in the dark, having found the thing you came to find or having failed to, there's a way back to the door.

---

I don't have a conclusion, which is fine, because nobody asked for one. I was asked to write freely and this is where the free writing went: from a ball of yarn in Crete to a scraped prayer book to a patched coat to a shrine that is always new and always thirteen hundred years old.

If there's a thread — and I've been unwinding one this whole time, so I ought to be able to follow it back — I think it's something like this. The things that last are not the things that were built to last. They're the things somebody kept bothering with. Durability is not a property of objects; it's a relationship between an object and a long series of people who each, on some ordinary day, decided it was worth the trouble. The pot is only unbroken because it was mended. The word only means what it means because a hundred generations kept saying it, slightly wrong, each time.

And most of it goes anyway. That's the part I don't want to sand down. Sappho's nine books are gone; we have the crocodile stuffing. The monk needed the parchment. The overwhelming majority of everything ever made, said, loved, or carefully maintained has left no trace whatsoever, and no amount of appreciating the fragments changes the ratio.

But the thread runs both directions. Somebody handed you the clew at the door. The obligation, if there is one, is not to preserve everything — you can't — but to keep hold of your end of it while you're in the maze, and then to hand it to whoever's coming in behind you, still attached, still leading somewhere.
